h1:
Samut Sakhon to Samut Prakan
Seafood Markets, Both Sides of the Gulf, in 2 Days
intro: These two provinces sit on opposite sides of the mouth of the Gulf of Thailand, but they're only about 45 km apart by road — take Rama II onto the ring road and you'll do it in under an hour, so pairing them into one trip is easy. The common thread is the sea: Samut Sakhon is known for fresh, cheap wholesale seafood markets, while Samut Prakan has the Pak Nam market on the Chao Phraya plus a mix of nature and history. Here's a relaxed 2-day, 1-night plan that hits the seafood markets on both shores.

blocks.html: People tend to forget Samut Sakhon and Samut Prakan are close, because they're on opposite sides of Bangkok and on different sides of the river. But if you skirt the city via Rama II and hop onto the southern section of the outer ring road, you'll get from one to the other in no time. So this trip has you sleep one night in Samut Sakhon, spend enough time on the seafood markets, then cross over to the Pak Nam side on day two.

The nice thing about this trip is that it suits people who drive themselves, because the seafood markets and several of the sights are spread out and not all of them sit next to a train line. Without a car you can still get around in stretches by van and songthaew, but you'll spend a lot more time changing between rides.

blocks.text: Why pair these two provinces together

items: Closer than you'd think — the two town centres are about 45 km apart, roughly a 40–60 minute drive depending on traffic. Skirt the city via Rama II onto the southern section of the outer ring road.

Same theme, different vibe — the Samut Sakhon side is fresh wholesale seafood at market prices, while the Samut Prakan side is markets along the Chao Phraya, outdoor nature, and an old temple out in the water.

Good morning and evening — the seafood markets on the Samut Sakhon side open early, while the Pak Nam market in Samut Prakan picks up from evening into the night, so you can time things so they don't clash.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Samut Sakhon and its seafood markets

items.activity: Start at Mahachai market (municipal pier) and walk the stalls of crab, shrimp and fresh short-bodied mackerel
items.note: The market runs from around 06:00 to 13:00. Come early while the catch is plentiful and fresh — you can grab breakfast around the market too.

items.activity: Take the Mahachai–Tha Chalom ferry across and walk the old Tha Chalom neighbourhood
items.note: The crossing takes just a few minutes and costs only a few baht. On the Tha Chalom side there's the old Thawai road and rows of old shophouses to walk and photograph.

items.activity: Pay respects at the Phan Thai Norasing Shrine and hear the legend of his loyalty
items.note: It's in Phan Thai Norasing subdistrict, and people often come to ask for blessings on their work. There are markets and restaurants around to stop at.

items.activity: Lunch on seafood at a local spot in Samut Sakhon town
items.note: Pick a place that's packed at midday. Mae Klong mackerel, blanched cockles and steamed blue crab are the local specialities around here.

items.activity: Walk Talay Thai, the large seafood market in Tha Chin subdistrict
items.note: Open daily from around 06:00 to 18:00, with both fresh and dried goods — dried squid, shrimp paste, fish sauce. Good for picking up things to take home.

items.activity: Pick up dried-seafood souvenirs, then check in to your hotel in town
items.note: Hotels in Mahachai come in a range of price points. Staying close to the town centre makes it easy to find dinner.

items.activity: Wrap up day one with a seafood dinner in Mahachai town
items.note: If you're not yet tired of it, try grilled prawns, cockles or seafood tom yum, then rest up for crossing provinces the next morning.

blocks.title: A tip about the seafood markets
blocks.html: Wholesale seafood markets have the best prices in the morning, when the catch is still fresh and the choice is widest. If you're buying fresh seafood to take home, bring a cooler with ice to be safe — especially on a hot day.

blocks.text: Day 2 — cross over to Samut Prakan and the Pak Nam side

blocks.html: On the morning of day two you leave Samut Sakhon and skirt the city over to the Samut Prakan side. You can go the nature route at Bang Krachao, or the history route with the Ancient City and Phra Samut Chedi, then finish at the Pak Nam market on the Chao Phraya.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Ancient City · Bang Krachao · Pak Nam market

items.activity: Leave Samut Sakhon and drive across to the Samut Prakan side
items.note: It's about 45 km, so allow an hour including traffic on Rama II, which has roadworks in places. Setting off a bit early makes it easier.

items.activity: Pick your route — the Ancient City, where you can see Thailand's landmarks in miniature across the whole country
items.note: The grounds are huge. You can rent a bike or a golf cart to get around, and you'll want at least 2–3 hours.

items.activity: Lunch around town, then on to Bang Krachao, the green lung in the river bend
items.note: Bang Krachao is great for an easy bike ride under the trees, and there's Bang Nam Phueng floating market, open Saturday–Sunday from around 08:00 to 14:00.

items.activity: Take the ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi, the in-water pagoda that's the symbol of the province
items.note: You can take the ferry across from the Pak Nam side. The riverside atmosphere on the Chao Phraya in the late afternoon is just right.

items.activity: Walk the Pak Nam market on the Chao Phraya, with fresh food and ready-to-eat covered
items.note: Pak Nam market has both fresh produce and food to eat, and it's easy to reach on the BTS green line to Pak Nam. The wholesale seafood stalls pick up from evening into the night.

items.activity: A riverside seafood dinner before heading back to Bangkok
items.note: Pick a spot on the Chao Phraya, watch the cargo boats pass, and close out a both-shores-of-the-Gulf trip on a full stomach.

blocks.text: Seafood markets on both shores — what to buy and where

items.name: Talay Thai market — Samut Sakhon
items.blurb: The province's large seafood market in Tha Chin subdistrict, with both fresh and dried goods. Good for buying in bulk or for dried-seafood souvenirs, shrimp paste and fish sauce.

items.name: Mahachai market (municipal pier) — Samut Sakhon
items.blurb: A fresh market in central Mahachai right by the pier, with crab, shrimp and short-bodied mackerel straight from the sea. Easy to walk in the town centre, and you can take the ferry across to Tha Chalom from here.

items.name: Pak Nam market — Samut Prakan
items.blurb: A market on the Chao Phraya in central Pak Nam, with fresh produce and food covered. The wholesale seafood stalls pick up from evening into the night, and it's easy to reach on the BTS to Pak Nam.
items.meta: Fresh market by day · wholesale in the evening to late

items.name: Khlong Dan seafood market — Samut Prakan
items.blurb: Out in Bang Bo district on the way to Chonburi, known for shrimp, mantis shrimp, blue crab and mud crab at fair prices. Worth a stop if you're driving on eastward.
items.meta: Out of town, Bang Bo district

blocks.html: The short version: if you want fresh seafood at market prices and plenty of choice, the Samut Sakhon side is the answer. If you'd rather stroll along the river and find something to eat as you go, the Pak Nam market in Samut Prakan gives you more of that Chao Phraya riverside-market feel.

blocks.text: Backup spots if you have time to spare

items.name: Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm
items.blurb: A large crocodile farm with crocodile shows and a zoo — good to bring the kids along.

items.name: Bang Pu Recreation Centre
items.blurb: Mangrove flats where you can watch the seagulls late in the year, plus the long Suk Ta pier walking out over the sea, with a cool, easy atmosphere.

items.name: Wat Chetsadaram
items.blurb: A royal temple in central Samut Sakhon — stop to pay respects and sample the sweets sold out front.

items.name: Khok Kham mangrove forest
items.blurb: A nature study trail through the mangroves, near the Phan Thai Norasing Shrine — good for those who like a nature walk.

blocks.text: What to know before you go

items: Driving yourself is easiest — the sights are spread out and not all next to a train line. Without a car, the Pak Nam side works on the BTS, but the Samut Sakhon side relies on vans and songthaews.
Rama II has roadworks — traffic backs up and lanes close in places, so allow extra travel time and check the route before you set off.
Keep fresh goods cold — if you're buying fresh seafood to take home, bring a cooler with ice and buy it near the end, right before you head back.

The markets run on different clocks — the Samut Sakhon seafood markets are best in the morning, while the wholesale stalls on the Pak Nam side pick up in the evening, so time your visits to match each market's rhythm.

faq.q: How far apart are Samut Sakhon and Samut Prakan, and is it a long drive?
faq.a: The two town centres are about 45 km apart, roughly a 40–60 minute drive depending on traffic. The main route skirts the city via Rama II onto the southern section of the outer ring road. There are roadworks in places along Rama II, so allow extra time.

faq.q: Which side has better seafood markets?
faq.a: The Samut Sakhon side stands out for fresh seafood at market prices and plenty of choice, especially Talay Thai and Mahachai markets. The Samut Prakan side — places like Pak Nam market — gives you the Chao Phraya riverside-market feel, while Khlong Dan market is known for shrimp and crab at good prices. Choose based on whether you want fresh produce or a riverside stroll.

faq.q: Can you do this trip in a single day?
faq.a: You can if you rush, but it'll be tiring and you won't fit everything in, because you have to cross provinces in the middle of the day. It's better to sleep one night in Mahachai, then cross to the Pak Nam side the next morning, so you can walk the seafood markets on both shores at an unhurried pace.

faq.q: Can you do this trip without your own car?
faq.a: You can, but it's harder. The Samut Prakan side has the BTS green line to Pak Nam, which makes walking the Pak Nam market easy. The Samut Sakhon side relies on vans and songthaews in stretches. If you want to hit all the seafood markets, driving yourself or renting a car is the most flexible.

faq.q: What time of day should you go to the seafood markets?
faq.a: Seafood markets on the Samut Sakhon side have the freshest catch and the widest choice in the morning. Mahachai market runs from around 06:00 to 13:00, and Talay Thai is open daily from around 06:00 to 18:00. On the Samut Prakan side, the wholesale stalls at Pak Nam market pick up from evening into the night.
